_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: I will exclude the blood of creeping animals, which do not have a severe impurity: for creeping animals do not render a person impure so as to render [his] clothing impure.
rashi:a1.2: Which is entirely permitted: he explains this below (21b).
rashi:a2.1: Of bird or of animal: why were both stated? For from one of them I could have derived [the rest] by “similar to the detail.”
rashi:a2.2: If, just as a bird, etc.: that is, if only “bird” had been stated, I would have said: just as a bird has no diverse kinds. He explains below [that this means] diverse kinds of wool, for a bird’s feathers are not subject to diverse kinds.
rashi:a2.3: So too an animal that has no [diverse kinds]: in its wool, such as an ox and a goat; one is liable for their blood, but not for the blood of sheep, since their wool is subject to diverse kinds.
rashi:a3.1: So too a bird that is not subject to [the law of] the mother with the young: such as a non-kosher bird, which does not require sending away [the mother]; one is liable for its blood, but not for kosher birds.
rashi:a7.1: The school of Rabbi Yishmael, who expound generalizations and details in a case like this: at the end of the chapter Elu Terefot (Ḥullin 66a), even though the first generalization is not similar to the last.
rashi:a10.1: To include a koy: an undomesticated animal did not need to be included, for an undomesticated animal is included in “animal,” in the chapter Behema HaMaksha (Ḥullin 71a), as Rabbi Yoḥanan explains there.
rashi:a10.2: Is a verse needed to forbid an uncertainty? This is a rhetorical question. For to what would we compare it? If to an undomesticated animal, its blood is forbidden; if to a domesticated animal, its blood is forbidden.
rashi:a11.1: Its carcass, from where do we derive it? [That is,] the prohibition against eating its carcass, from where do we derive it?
rashi:a12.1: The Merciful One made it depend on the spoon of the thigh: for anything that has a “spoon” (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), the sciatic nerve applies to it. And the reason it does not apply to a bird is explained in the chapter Gid HaNashe (Ḥullin 92b): its “spoon” is not round.
rashi:a13.1: Its impurity: that its carcass imparts impurity.
rashi:a14.1: “Require intent and susceptibility”: this is how we read it in tractate Okatzin.
rashi:a15.1: Let his cutting count as intent: since he cut it, he showed he regarded it [as food], so that if impurity touched it, it would receive impurity.
rashi:a21.1: The carcass of a non-kosher animal anywhere: even in marketplaces, where there are many people, it requires intent for eating in order to receive the impurity of food, since it is not usually eaten.
rashi:a21.2: And likewise the carcass of a kosher bird in villages: where the people are few, they require intent for the impurity of food.
rashi:a21.3: And they do not require susceptibility: because they impart a severe impurity. The carcass of an animal imparts impurity through carrying, and the carcass of a kosher bird renders clothing impure [when it is] in the throat [as it is swallowed]; and we say below that anything that will ultimately impart a severe impurity does not require susceptibility.
rashi:a21.4: Here we do not read “and the fat”: even though the mishna teaches it in the case of marketplaces, which implies that in villages it requires intent, it does not teach it in the first clause, since one could not teach of it that it does not require susceptibility. For if it means the fat of a carcass, it requires susceptibility, since it does not impart a severe impurity; and if it means the fat of a slaughtered animal, since it is in villages it is not rendered susceptible by the blood of the slaughter, for susceptibility that comes before intent is not [effective] susceptibility, as we say in the chapter HaOr VeHaRotev (Ḥullin 128a): chicory that one gathered for an animal and then decided to use for people requires a second susceptibility. This mishna is at the end of tractate Okatzin.
rashi:a22.1: The carcass of a kosher animal anywhere: even in villages, where the people are few, they do not require intent, for ordinarily it is meant to be eaten by gentiles. And likewise the carcass of a kosher bird, and the fat of a domesticated or undomesticated animal, in marketplaces, where the people are many.
rashi:a22.2: They require neither intent nor susceptibility: for the carcass of an animal and of a bird impart a severe impurity; and the fat here is the fat of a slaughtered animal, which was already rendered susceptible by the blood of the slaughter.
rashi:a23.1: But it itself is impure: with the impurity of carcasses.
rashi:a23.2: In less than an olive-bulk there is no impurity of carcasses, and when he intends it for eating, it combines with less than an egg-bulk of food for the impurity of food.
rashi:a24.1: If so: that it is less than an olive-bulk and will never come to the impurity of carcasses, let it also require susceptibility, for the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught, etc.
tosafot:a1.1: I will exclude the blood of creeping animals, which do not have a severe impurity: even though it imparts impurity through contact, it does not impart impurity through carrying, nor [does it render] clothing [impure].
tosafot:a1.2: I will exclude the blood of eggs of a bird, which are not a type of meat: Rabbeinu Barukh found it puzzling that [the baraita] does not exclude all of them on one ground, [such as] “and they have the forbidden and the permitted”; and the blood of eggs and of grasshoppers it could have excluded because they have no severe impurity. Rather, [the reason it gives] is the plainer one for them, [as with] the permission that the Talmud states.
tosafot:a10.1: A koy is a distinct entity: in the chapter Oto VeEt Beno (Ḥullin 80a), which teaches, “A koy is a distinct entity, and the Sages did not decide whether it is a kind of undomesticated or domesticated animal,” that “entity” is not like the “entity” here. For the entity there is either a domesticated or an undomesticated kind, since it says “and the Sages did not decide about it.” But here it means a distinct entity that is neither an undomesticated nor a domesticated animal, for if it were one of them, its blood would not have needed to be included. And likewise in Yoma (74a), “Any fat, to include a koy and a half-measure,” where it says, “A koy is a distinct entity,” it does not mean that it is an uncertain case, either undomesticated or domesticated, for then a verse would not be needed to forbid its fat.
tosafot:a15.1: When he cut it for a dog: it could equally have answered “when he cut it for medicine,” but this teaches us that even when he cut it for a dog it requires intent.
tosafot:a23.1: For example, where there is less than an olive-bulk of a carcass and he combined it: but one cannot say [that he combined] an olive-bulk, and that intent is effective so that this egg-bulk renders other foods impure even when the foods touch only the combined [food] and not the carcass. For then it would not explain [the baraita’s] “just as an animal has a light impurity,” which implies that there is a carcass that has only the impurity of food; and if it were an olive-bulk, it would have a severe impurity. Furthermore, one can say that it is implied by the mishna cited here, “the carcass of a non-kosher animal anywhere, and the carcass of a kosher bird…”: this implies that the carcass of the animal is like the carcass of the bird, that is, that it requires intent just as the bird does; and therefore he chose less than an olive-bulk.
gershom:a1.1: And creeping animals have no severe impurity: for they do not impart impurity through carrying, since “and one who carries their carcass” is not written of them.
gershom:a2.1: I will exclude the blood of eggs of a bird, which are not a type of meat. Fish and grasshoppers, which are entirely permitted: for they do not require slaughter.
gershom:a3.1: Of bird or of animal: [the Gemara] infers: why did it write both? Let it derive from one. From “bird”: [had only “bird” been written,] I would have said: just as a bird has no diverse kinds, for its feathers are not forbidden either with wool or with linen, and its blood is forbidden, so too an animal whose wool is not subject to the prohibition of diverse kinds, such as a goat and a cow, its blood is forbidden, but not sheep. That is why “or of animal” is written: to forbid the blood of every animal.
gershom:a4.1: And had only “animal” been written, I would have said: just as an animal is not subject to the prohibition “you shall not take the mother with the young,” and its blood is forbidden, so too a bird that is not subject to the prohibition of the mother with the young, such as one that is at hand [mezuman] or a non-kosher bird; to exclude the blood of a kosher bird that is not at hand. [Therefore] the verse states “of bird.”
gershom:a5.1: But say “any blood” is a generalization, etc.: the generalization includes only what is in the detail, bird and animal, yes; anything else, no, so as to exclude the blood of an undomesticated animal. [The answer:] It is written, “any soul that eats any blood”: it generalized again. It is a generalization, a detail and a generalization, and you may derive only what is similar to the detail; and this is as we said above: just as bird and animal are unique, etc.
gershom:a6.1: But it is not similar, etc.: what of it? We find that the tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael expounds amplifications and limitations in the chapter Elu Terefot (Ḥullin 66a) [a printed note: Rabbeinu Gershom’s reading was “who expound amplifications and limitations, and generalizations and details, in such a case,” as in the other version cited in the Shitta Mekubbetzet here], and generalizations and details in the chapter Merubeh (Bava Kamma 64a), even though they are not similar to each other. Here too we expound a generalization, a detail and a generalization even though they are not similar, and the blood of an undomesticated animal and of a koy is included.
gershom:a7.1: So too every, to include the blood of a koy. The blood of an undomesticated animal did not need to be included, for the prohibition of blood is written of it explicitly: it is written, “And any man who hunts an undomesticated animal,” and after it is written, “You shall not eat the blood of any flesh.” And if he holds that a koy is possibly an undomesticated animal and possibly a domesticated one, is a verse needed to include it and forbid an uncertainty? Obviously its blood is forbidden either way.
gershom:a8.1: Rather, he holds that a koy is a distinct entity, and a verse was needed to include it and forbid its blood.
gershom:a9.1: From “for whoever eats fat,” read into it [a printed note: it seems this should read, “read into it ‘whoever eats any fat’: ‘any,’ even of a koy.” The note adds that this is hard to understand, since the Talmud can derive it from the verse “any fat” in Leviticus 3, where “any fat” itself is written, and leaves it for further study]: “for whoever eats fat,” “any,” even of a koy. Its carcass, from where do we derive it? That it is forbidden to eat: from “any” in “you shall not eat any carcass.”
gershom:a10.1: One who cuts from a person: from a living person, flesh for the sake of eating.
gershom:a11.1: Requires intent: if he intended it for eating, it imparts the impurity of food in an egg-bulk. And it does not require susceptibility; even without susceptibility it becomes impure, since we hold that anything that will ultimately become impure with a severe impurity does not require susceptibility.
gershom:a12.1: Let his cutting count as intent: since he cut it, he regarded it [as food].
gershom:a13.1: Reish Lakish said: [it is a case] where he did not cut it simply for a person but for a dog, for intent for the needs of a dog is not intent.
gershom:a14.1: And not? But didn’t we learn: they stated a principle in Teharot: anything designated as food for a person is impure with the impurity of food until it is rendered unfit for a dog to eat. Evidently eating by a dog counts. [The answer:] What we said, “until it is rendered unfit for a dog to eat,” is for removing it from impurity: we measure by a dog, since it was originally fit for a person.
gershom:a15.1: Here we are dealing with bringing it into the impurity of food, in one who cuts from a living person: if it is fit for a person, that is, he intended it for a person to eat, it is fit for a dog; and if it is not fit for a person, that is, he did not intend it as food for a person but for a dog, it is not fit for a dog, for we do not bring it into the impurity of food on account of a dog.
gershom:a16.1: In any case it teaches intent: and intent is needed for a light impurity, to impart the impurity of food.
gershom:a17.1: This applies, that it teaches “requires intent,” during life, when it does not impart a severe impurity. But one who cuts from it after death, since it is impure with a severe impurity, it has no light impurity. [A printed note: it seems this should read, “And it challenges: if the baraita deals with after death…”] And in the sense that the baraita deals with after death, [saying] “the blood of bipeds is excluded,” correspondingly with an animal it deals with after death, and even so it has a light impurity. In what does it have a light impurity? If flesh, it imparts a severe impurity in an olive-bulk through carrying; and if blood, it too imparts a severe impurity.
gershom:a18.1: And Beit Hillel deem it impure: when there is a quarter-log of it, since it can congeal and stand at an olive-bulk, as it says in the chapter HaMenaḥot.
gershom:a19.1: Rather, it is necessary only: [to teach] that an animal after death has the impurity of food, as we learned: the carcass of a non-kosher animal anywhere, since it is not fit to be eaten by anyone, Jews or gentiles; and likewise the carcass of a bird, even a kosher one, and the fat and the suet in villages, whose people are not wealthy and do not eat birds or suet, since they set it aside for a lamp or for work. These require intent to impart the impurity of food, since they are not fit for everyone to eat; and they do not require susceptibility, as we said: anything that will ultimately become impure with a severe impurity does not require susceptibility.
gershom:a20.1: And Rav said to Rabbi Ḥiyya: intent, for what? If for a light impurity, it itself imparts a severe impurity in an olive-bulk.
gershom:a21.1: And he said to him: intent is needed for this: for example, where there is less than an olive-bulk of a carcass, which does not impart a severe impurity, and he combined it with other food of less than an egg-bulk. That is why it requires intent: because it does not have the measure for a severe impurity.
gershom:a22.1: If so, let it require susceptibility. [The answer:] But here, where there is less than an olive-bulk of carcass among them, since if he combined it into an olive-bulk with the rest of the body of the carcass it would not require susceptibility, for it imparts a severe impurity, now too, even though it is less than an olive-bulk, it does not require susceptibility, but it does require intent.
rashi:b1.1: To the exclusion of a corpse: that is, this is why we said above, “bipeds are excluded, as they have no light impurity”: even though he fills less than an egg-bulk of food with less than an olive-bulk of a corpse, it does not combine with it for the impurity of food, because his intention is rendered irrelevant by [that of] all people.
rashi:b2.1: That he covered it with dough: less than an egg-bulk, and this [carcass] completes it to an egg-bulk. Even though [the carcass] itself is impure, combining is effective for it, since now it does not impart impurity through contact, for it is covered. And when he says it combines with the dough for the impurity of food, there is an egg-bulk of impure food, and it renders impure other foods that touch it.
rashi:b3.1: If so: that it is covered and will not ultimately impart a severe impurity, let it also require susceptibility.
rashi:b4.1: To the exclusion of a corpse: this is why it teaches above, “bipeds have no light impurity”: for if he covered it with dough, the severe impurity breaks through and ascends. For with any covering over a corpse that has no empty space of a handbreadth, the impurity breaks through and ascends, as we say in the chapter HaOr VeHaRotev (Ḥullin 125a).
rashi:b5.1: The Master said: creeping animals are excluded, etc.: it seems to me that we should not read this passage, in which it answers “but it does not impart impurity through carrying,” for a bird too does not impart impurity through carrying, and yet it said above that it imparts a severe impurity.
rashi:b9.1: Undomesticated animals and birds are like them: in Bava Kamma, in the chapter Shor SheNagaḥ et HaPara (Bava Kamma 54b): “Both an ox and any animal [are equal] with regard to falling into a pit… and with regard to diverse kinds and Shabbat; and likewise undomesticated animals and birds are like them.”
rashi:b11.1: One is flogged for it: [the Gemara] at first supposes [that he means] because of [the prohibition of] blood.
rashi:b11.2: By a prohibition: and not by karet, since it is not the blood of the soul [i.e., the lifeblood]. (This comment is printed in brackets in the Vilna Rashi.)
rashi:b11.3: And one is not liable for it: [not liable to] lashes.
rashi:b13.1: One, that this is the first clause: for if so, what difference is there between the blood of bipeds [so the printed text, in parentheses] and the blood of limbs, and why did it divide them into two statements?
rashi:b13.2: And furthermore, this tanna above excludes it from a prohibition too, as it teaches: the blood of creeping animals is excluded, from the general [verse] “you shall not eat any blood.”
rashi:b14.1: If they forewarned him due to a creeping animal, he is flogged: as we say in the first chapter (Keritot 4b above): “And these are impure to you” teaches about the blood of a creeping animal and its flesh, that they combine to an olive-bulk for eating. Evidently the blood of creeping animals is like their flesh.
rashi:b15.1: That he collected: in a vessel, it is forbidden, since it may be confused with the blood of an animal, and someone who sees it will say it is permitted to eat blood.
rashi:b15.2: The blood of fish and grasshoppers is permitted even ab initio: this is the latter clause of that baraita which was taught above, “blood of the spleen, blood of the heart, etc.”
rashi:b16.1: Correspondingly with bipeds: where this middle clause teaches “forbidden, but one is not liable for it,” you would also establish it where he did not collect it, since that is how you answered the latter clause of the baraita.
rashi:b16.2: Blood on a loaf: even though it is not like [blood] that one collected, and there is no prohibition, there is nevertheless a command to abstain from it. But that between the teeth, which is still attached, has not even a command to abstain; he sucks it without concern, and it is not like [blood] that one collected.
rashi:b17.1: That has [scales] in it: blood with scales in it is permitted ab initio, since it will not be confused with the blood of a domesticated animal, an undomesticated animal or a bird.
rashi:b18.2: There is not even a command to abstain in it: there is no mitzva to abstain from it, not even as a mere command of abstention.
tosafot:b2.1: Rav Ḥananya said: you may even say, etc.: he was not satisfied to establish it as Rabbi Ḥiyya did, for it is forced to say “since if he combined it into an olive-bulk [it would not require susceptibility], therefore it does not require susceptibility”; for one could equally say now, “since if it were not covered with dough it would not require susceptibility,” etc. So he did not want to answer like Rabbi Ḥiyya, but answers that even now it imparts impurity through carrying. Furthermore, Rabbi Ḥiyya’s explanation is forced in that the severe impurity and the light impurity are in two places: the severe impurity in an olive-bulk and the light impurity in less than an olive-bulk. But Rav Ḥananya finds both in one place, in an olive-bulk that he covered with dough: the severe [impurity] through carrying, and the light through its contact. And his words “you may even say that it is an olive-bulk” are not precise, for they imply that he fully agrees about less than an olive-bulk, and that is not so, as we explained.
tosafot:b16.1: In brief: The Gemara asks: correspondingly with the blood of bipeds where he did not collect it, is it forbidden? That is, the same baraita that permits fish blood teaches “the blood of bipeds is forbidden,” and yet another baraita lets one suck blood from between the teeth, and Rashi explains that this has not even a command to abstain. Tosafot explain why Rashi needed this: otherwise there would be no challenge, since blood between the teeth has not separated and is not seen, whereas blood that separated is forbidden even uncollected, as with the blood on the loaf that one scrapes off; so Rashi says the loaf has only a command to abstain, and the challenge is that Rav said “forbidden” while here, though seen and separated, there is only a command to abstain. Tosafot object: a command to abstain is itself a full prohibition, so the challenge would rest only on the latter clause, and one could answer that blood between the teeth differs because it has not separated, while separated human blood is forbidden even uncollected (and correspondingly blood on a fish is permitted even when it has separated). Or perhaps one sucks and swallows it because it is known to come from the teeth, while “the blood of bipeds is forbidden” is where its source is not known; but blood dripping from one’s finger is permitted, since it is known to come from there and cannot be mistaken for the blood of a domesticated or undomesticated animal. Rabbeinu Barukh answers that the challenge runs thus: had fish blood been permitted even when collected, and human blood forbidden, the novelty would be that human blood is forbidden even when collected, and it would be fine that the baraita teaches no permitted case of human blood. But once Rav holds collected fish blood forbidden, the baraita speaks of uncollected blood, so it should have taught the permitted side of human blood, as it did for fish, if there were one; this implies human blood has no permitted case at all, even unseparated. Hence the challenge from blood between the teeth, which one sucks without concern: if that is permitted, the baraita should have drawn the distinction for human blood. The answer, that the baraita speaks of fish blood with scales, explains why no permission is taught for human blood, to which scales do not apply. From here it follows that fish blood is forbidden only when collected and without scales. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b18.1: It raises an objection: blood of the spleen, etc., these are by a prohibition: and in any case it raises the objection; but there is no karet [for these].
gershom:b1.1: [A printed note: up to here belongs to the previous amud.] To the exclusion of a dead person: even though he fills up less than an olive-bulk of it and completes it with an egg-bulk of food, it does not impart the impurity of food, even though he intends to eat it, because his intention is rendered irrelevant by [that of] all people, for people do not usually eat a dead person. And that is why it says, “the blood of bipeds is excluded,” etc.
gershom:b2.1: Rav Ḥananya said: you may even say that it is: here, an olive-bulk of the carcass of a non-kosher animal. And if you say: but it itself is impure with a severe impurity, in an olive-bulk, through contact —
gershom:b3.1: What are we dealing with here? Where he covered it with dough all around, so that it cannot touch [anything], and completed it to an egg-bulk with that dough. And if you say: if so, since it does not impart impurity through contact, let it require susceptibility like other foods —
gershom:b4.1: This applies, that susceptibility is required, to other food that does not impart impurity, etc. Through carrying, at any rate, it imparts impurity, for it cannot be carried [without imparting impurity]; therefore it does not require susceptibility. To the exclusion of an olive-bulk of a corpse: even though he covered it with dough, it imparts a severe impurity, even through contact, for we say it breaks through and ascends. Therefore the blood of bipeds is excluded, since they have no light impurity.
gershom:b5.1: But didn’t we learn in Bava Kamma: and undomesticated animals and birds are like them? That an animal [is subject to these laws] for plowing, for mating, for unloading, etc.
gershom:b6.1: Rather, Abaye said: that its wool: [that is, the feathers] of a bird; one is not liable for it due to diverse kinds if he combined it with linen.
gershom:b7.1: Blood of the spleen, blood of the heart, blood of the kidneys, blood of a limb, that came out of them.
gershom:b8.1: One, that this is the first clause: for if in any case one is liable for a prohibition, this is the first clause; let it combine them and teach them together: the blood of limbs, the blood of bipeds, and the blood of creeping and crawling things are forbidden, but one is not liable for them. And furthermore, the tanna at the beginning of our chapter excludes it from a prohibition too, as it teaches, “I will exclude the blood of creeping animals” from the prohibition “you shall not eat,” “for they have no severe impurity.”
gershom:b9.1: Rather, Rabbi Zeira said: it is not difficult. If they forewarned him, when he ate the blood of a creeping animal, due to the prohibition of the creeping animal itself, he is flogged for it in an olive-bulk; but if they forewarned him due to the blood of a creeping animal, he is not flogged, as the baraita teaches. And furthermore, its blood is distinct from its flesh.
gershom:b10.1: That he collected: that he gathered it on purpose, an olive-bulk or more than an olive-bulk; it is forbidden.
gershom:b11.1: Correspondingly with the blood of bipeds: for this baraita itself, in the Tosefta, teaches, “and the blood of bipeds is also forbidden.” And if you say it too is where he did not collect it, is it forbidden?
gershom:b12.1: But isn’t it taught: blood on a loaf, which came out of a person’s teeth, he scrapes it off and eats the loaf; and blood between the teeth, which has not come out, he sucks and swallows without concern, for there is no prohibition in it, since he did not collect it.
gershom:b13.1: Rather: the fish [blood] of the baraita deals with where he collected it, and it is not difficult: when the baraita teaches “permitted even ab initio,” it is where there are scales in the blood, so that it is recognizable as fish blood and will not be confused.
